Biophilic architecture and designs for mental well-being
Meredian Alam
Department of Sociology and Anthropology, Universiti Brunei Darussalam, Brunei.
meredian.alam@ubd.edu.bn
Abstract. There is a growing recognition that people who stay in contact with nature are more
likely to enjoy fulfilling, fruitful lives. More recently, architects and designers have begun to
recognize the importance of biophilic design, which incorporates natural elements into built
environments. However, as urbanization spreads around the globe, attention must be redirected
to city size, with an emphasis on planning for and making progress toward "biophilic cities."
Biophilic communities are ones that aim to foster a sense of appreciation and stewardship for the
natural world among their citizens by providing them with enough opportunities to experience
nature both inside and beyond the city limits. Employing deconstructive discourse analysis on
different uses of biophilic concepts, the present paper aims to review the contribution of biophilic
architecture and designs to the improved physical space for mental well-being.
1. Introduction
In 1964, social scientist Erich Fromm initially used the term "biophilia" to support the idea that humans
have an innate need for connection with other forms of life [1,2]. Several research studies have shown
that severing this link might cause physical and psychological health problems. As a result of applying
a psychologically derived idea to building design, "biophilic architecture" became a heavily researched
topic in the literature [3], particularly since the 2000s. While sustainable design takes a more material
and physically oriented approach to the natural processes humans need, biophilic design focuses on the
psychological and emotional aspects of people's needs to engage with the natural environment [4].
Sustainable design reduces the environmental effect of buildings but does not re-establish human-nature
interaction. Biophilic architecture is an attempt to fill this need [5]. This approach takes a human-
centered, sustainability-focused approach to the biophilia phenomena, focusing on people's physical and
mental well-being as the primary concern.
Most of the world's population now lives in urban areas, where they are cut off from nature and are
more likely to suffer from stress-related ailments such as decreased productivity, chronic fatigue,
depression, etc. With 70% of the world's population likely to live in cities in the following years, re-
establishing the human-nature bond and presenting nature as a rehabilitation tool for urbanists will be
important [6]. More than half of humanity currently lives in cities as of 2007. Urbanization and the
elimination of green space and natural surroundings as a result of a rise in the number of city dwellers
worldwide are two consequences of this trend [7]. To preserve, maintain, restore, and improve our
physiological, cognitive, and psychological ties to the natural world, "biophilic design" seeks to reinstate
natural stimuli in our constructed and created settings. Biophilic design can stimulate landscape
architecture’s involvement in urban public health as part of a salutogenic approach to health [8].
Meanwhile, mass urbanization is a major problem of the 21st century. It is particularly crucial to restoring
urban rivers in light of the effects of climate change [9], which have been exacerbated by urbanization

and the resulting increase in ground sealing. Biophilic design patterns were developed to increase city
well-being and resilience long-term [10]. The advantages of a regenerative economy and a holistic
perspective are shown by the fact that such measures will improve inhabitants' health, social cohesion,
and well-being while simultaneously lowering their exposure to climate change hazards like the heat
island effect and flash floods [11].
In tandem with the fields of architecture and construction, mental health concerns related to the
constructed and interior environment are examined in light of their relationship to the outdoors [1].
Biophilic design has gained momentum in the past four decades and is now seen as a way to bridge the
gap between people and nature. Biophilic design focuses on the end results of organically inspired
dwellings and workspaces. It encompasses green and intelligent construction practices, serves as a
countermeasure to a toxic indoor atmosphere, and articulates the belief that true sustainability can only
be attained by exercising qualitative control over people's physical well-being and mental health [12].
In terms of work efficiency, preference, and productivity in an indoor setting, it is seen as a way to
encourage creative and positive thinking. This article aims to present biophilic design and retrofitting
solutions, which may enhance cognitive performance, lessen stress, and promote emotional well-being
in man-made spaces.
Methodologically speaking, the present study employs deconstructive discourse analysis. This
method allows the authors to explore the chronological trajectories of biophilic architecture spanning its
common practices, uses, and the progress of its applications. The primary literature examined for this
method is those of relevant publications, including articles, archives, and essays highlighting biophilia.
2. Contributions of biophilic designs to improved mental health: From concepts to practices
Bringing more nature and natural components into a prison has been shown to lower stress, enhance
inmates' mental health, cognitive functioning, and learning, decrease recidivism and make inmates more
amenable to behavioral reform and restorative justice programs. The term "biophilic design" refers to a
group of ideas emphasizing the integration of natural elements into urban environments and the everyday
lives of city dwellers [13]. Collectively, the techniques should enhance prison life. There are a variety
of up-and-coming design techniques, like biophilic design, which draw inspiration from and model their
processes after those found in nature to enhance the quality of the surrounding environment, human
health, and productivity [14]. As it may function as a platform offering a connective vocabulary,
practice, and ethos that can combine different activities in the built environment more generally,
biophilic design incorporates the contributions of other nature-based design methodologies without
usurping them. The built environment consists of where people live, work, and play regularly, including
our cities, neighborhoods, workplaces, and houses. Several studies have examined how our built
environment influences our health, well-being, and quality of life [7]. Biophilic design, an offshoot of
biophilia, is a novel approach to design that aspires to cultivate a profound connection with nature in
settings such as our homes, schools, and places of work [15]. The purpose of this article is to provide a
comprehensive overview of the state of biophilic design as it pertains to the kinds of indoor
environments where people spend the majority of their time.
Urban planners and architects should consider the need for people to experience psychological
renewal by including natural settings in their projects. Based on our preliminary research, we conclude
that metropolitan settings and buildings may also be high on interest, which is consistent with the
Attention Restoration Theory's claim that such surroundings improve performance, mood, and well-
being by drawing effortless involuntary focus while requiring minimal deliberate attention [16].
Intentional design informed by an understanding of how humans are wired to respond to the natural
world may also provide feelings of contentment (biophilic architecture) [17]. People's appreciation for
the beauty of the natural world stems not only from the physical components of the natural world but
also from the human ability to recreate the features and attributes of the natural world in man-made
structures. The cognitive comfort of a landscape has less to do with any particular aspect than with the
interplay between natural and man-made ones [18]. When it comes to boosting people's mental health,

3. Urban biophilic designs for urbanites
Biophilic design is an emerging field that uses the latest research on the human-nature connection to
create built environments more in tune with people's natural inclination toward biophilia. The benefits
of biophilic design in alleviating stress, fostering innovation and clarity of thought, enhancing health on
all levels, and speeding recovery are all well-documented [20]. The promotion of biophilia design
philosophy is passed down by providing concrete evidence for lifestyle centers' healing powers [21].
Retail landscapes that include groomed gardens, plants, fountains, and pathways lined with hip stores,
restaurants, and nightlife venues are becoming more popular worldwide [22]. Following attention
restoration theory (ART), it is discovered that there is a causal relationship between biophilic design and
human health, namely the alleviation of mental tiredness. The consistency of biophilia design is further
shown by a series of research that probe shoppers' reactions to natural components in relation to their
purchasing motivations (window shopping vs. planned purchases) and whether they are paying full or
reduced pricing [23]. This research reveals the healing potential of lifestyle and its transforming
significance in improving individual and social well-being. There is mounting evidence that connecting
with nature improves mental health and overall well-being. Nowadays, the vast majority of humans live
in metropolitan areas, where they spend little time outside [24]. Consequently, it is crucial to investigate
methods for incorporating more natural elements into urban settings. Biophilic design refers to an
approach to design that takes into account humans' intrinsic need for and interest in the natural
environment. In this study, we develop a novel biophilic urbanism paradigm for evaluating and charting
these features in urban environments. Wellington, New Zealand, was mapped based on 30 features
identified as indicative of biophilic urban environments [25]. Access to the wild environment may be
an essential component of a biophilic city, but deliberate design interventions are also vital [25]. When
biophilic elements are part of a wider integrated spatial experience across time, beneficial impacts may
be reinforced. This may help pinpoint prime spots for biophilic interventions in the city's larger fabric,
paving the way for more efficient urban nature encounters [26]. Given this, it stands to reason that a
biophilic approach to urban planning should take into account the whole range of human senses.
Given the unrelenting rate of urbanization worldwide, these advantages will only grow in
significance as we plan our cities, buildings, and homes. This project aims to bridge the gap between
basic scientific inquiry and practical application by constructing a theoretical foundation for biophilic
design. In one study, biophilic design patterns and design must involve elements such as natural imagery,
plant life, linkages to nature both visually and non-visually, and natural materials [27]. These
investigations have some bearing on physiology and psychology, either immediately or by a circuitous
route involving contact with the natural world or the subjective experience of travel [28]. Recently,
architecture researchers in Australia have been conducting a long-term study to determine whether or
not construction site offices including biophilic design positively affect employees' health and
productivity [29]. A custom site design included an open plan workplace, natural lighting, ventilation,
abundant plants, vistas and views, recycled materials, and non-synthetic materials. In the first three
months, information was collected via interviews with site personnel and a questionnaire focusing on
demographics. Incorporating biophilic design elements has been shown to significantly impact
productivity, stress levels, well-being, workplace collaboration, and job satisfaction, all of which
contribute to a high-performance workplace.
4. Influence of biophilic design on psychological well-being
While the effect of architecture and interior design on human health and productivity has been
extensively explored in places like hospitals and primary schools, more research is needed on the impact
of biopsychosocial and biophilic design in urban higher education institutions [30]. Implementing
health-promoting and restorative environmental design solutions may help university students overcome

some of the particular issues they experience and positively impact their lives and education. Emotional
stress, happiness, stimulation, cognitive function, social support, belonging, study spaces, lighting, and
ventilation are all identified as important topics in the published multi-disciplinary research about the
built environment's impact on university students [12]. The semi-structured literature review identifies,
evaluates, and categorizes important research on nature views, nature pictures, natural colors, natural
materials, auditory and olfactory components of nature, nature images with water, indoor plants, campus
landscapes, study spaces, local materials, and style, daylight access, thermal and environmental comfort
[30]. While it is common knowledge that exposure to nature may positively affect health and
productivity, further research is required to determine the optimal greenery dosage and its associated
well-being advantages for use in design practice. In this research, we looked at the physiological,
psychological, and performance effects of varying greenery levels in the office. The health and
productivity of 15 participants were assessed using cutting-edge gadgets, questionnaires, and activities
as part of a repeated-measures experiment testing zero, 0.2 percent, five percent, twelve percent, and
twenty percent green coverage ratios. Participants were also subjected to eye tracking tests to confirm
that the favorable effects on health and productivity resulted from their prolonged exposure to visually
appealing vegetation scenes. Employees worked harder and more efficiently in every situation where
plants were present. However, the percentage of green covering is either too low (0.2%) or too high
(20%) to have a restorative impact on people's mental state [32]. Similarly, merely 12 to 20 percent
green covering had a favorable effect on physiological brain processes. After considering the effects of
greenery on employees' minds, bodies, and ability to get work done, we settled on a ratio of 12 percent
green covering as the sweet spot. Given that the green coverage ratio is one of the most crucial design
criteria, the results of this study give not only essential measurement datasets for quantitative biophilic
design research but also crucial insights to back up biophilic design practice. Parasympathetic nerve
systems may be favorably influenced, cognitive functions can be enhanced, and attention can be focused
by exposure to natural surroundings, even through the sight of photographs. This research looked at how
college students in a residential academic environment in the northeastern United States rated their own
sense of well-being, taking into account factors including their ability to cope, their sense of self-worth,
and their physical health [33]. Compared to male students, female students reported lower levels of
resilience, poorer self-esteem, and a diminished capacity to select favorable health practices. The results
indicate that the physical environment on a university campus might support students and nurture them
throughout the academic year by including biophilic components.
5. Biophilic design for co-improving physical conditions
Because of reduced physiological function and minimal engagement in social activities, the elderly are
more prone to suffer passive emotions such as loneliness, anxiety, and sadness [30,34]. As a result, this
research aims to discover ways to integrate biophilic design into the residential area for the elderly from
a healing viewpoint while keeping mental health in mind. Because of its emphasis on natural
components and consideration for human comfort, biophilic design has been shown to improve people's
mental health and well-being [35]. This research has significance because it focuses on a key component
of the biophilic design pattern: creating a restorative environment for the elderly by combining a pleasant
view of the outdoors with their living quarters. The demand for assisted living facilities has grown due
to the aging population, the rising cost of living, and the changes in family composition. These areas are
governed by rules, although no universally applicable layout or design standards exist. This research
examines biophilia, biophilic design, and universal design patterns. Based on the findings, an assessment
is made. The seven universal design criteria and fourteen biophilic design patterns are examined jointly.
Rockwood Retirement South Hill, an outstanding project, met the pattern requirements in the table to a
large degree [36]. The biophilic design standards, shown to have a favorable effect on users across
psychological, physiological, and social domains, and the universal design criteria, which are both
simple access for the elderly, are assessed in this research.
The concept of biophilic design, which blends aspects of nature into the built environment, has been
gaining popularity in recent years [21]. Although there is some evidence that being among interior

biophilic elements may improve health and productivity, this evidence is limited. Researching how
office workers' bodies and minds react to exposure to nature's elements, this randomized crossover
research was conducted. Twenty-eight individuals were randomly assigned to spend time in either an
indoor setting with biophilic design components or one without. Every time they came, they spent 5
minutes there, both in the actual world and in a virtual one (VR) [37]. Blood pressure, galvanic skin
reaction, and heart rate were measured via wearable sensors. After each treatment, the subjects were
given a battery of cognitive tests. Participants' blood pressure was shown to be lower when exposed to
a biophilic indoor environment. Overall, those exposed to a biophilic indoor environment had 8.6 mmHg
lower systolic blood pressure and 3.6 mmHg lower diastolic blood pressure than those who were not.
When exposed to a biophilic environment, participants saw a higher reduction in skin conductance (0.18
uS) compared to the non-biophilic condition. The improvement in short-term memory was 14% [38].
After witnessing the biophilic atmosphere, participants reported a reduction in negative feelings and an
increase in pleasant emotions. Furthermore, the results argue that people who experienced a biophilic
habitat had almost identical physiological and cognitive reactions as those who experienced the natural
environment. This raises the prospect of lowering stress and boosting cognition by employing virtual
reality to offer exposure to natural elements in a range of interior situations where access to the outdoors
may be limited [32]. According to the investigational analysis of research literature, there is a rising
trend to create these healing spaces by reconnecting individuals to nature. It is based on a lot of research
and analysis of why industrialized hospitals do not work and how turning back to nature using
Restorative Environmental Design (RED) principles can help both the people who use the building and
the environment around it [39]. This study employs a hybrid approach of literature analysis and case
study to propose a new design framework that combines the ideas of salutogenic and biophilic design
to harness the therapeutic influence of the connection with nature to reduce people's misery, sadness,
anxiety, and pain. The framework's application is shown by examining the design of the Royal Children's
Hospital in Melbourne, Australia. The finding suggests that the framework has the potential for bringing
biophilic design to the design community; nevertheless, more empirical and practical evaluation is
required to fully investigate the effects of such patterns.
6. Conclusions
To summarize, there is an increasing awareness of the need to maintain regular contact with natural
environments to lead joyful and productive lives. This power of nature has recently been acknowledged
by architects and designers who have been paying more attention to biophilic architecture. However,
the growing urbanization of the world necessitates a shift in focus on the size of cities, with an emphasis
on planning for and progressing toward "biophilic cities.” Biophilic cities are cities that not only give
residents frequent and intimate interaction with nature, as well as nature located in close proximity to
the city, but also attempt to cultivate an awareness of and a concern for the natural environment. It is
stated in this article that cities that prioritize biodiversity also tend to be resilient and environmentally
responsible. Realizing the conditions of a biophilic city will go a long way toward helping to develop
social and landscape resilience in the face of climate change, natural catastrophes, economic instability,
and several other types of shocks that cities may experience in the future. The present article has
outlined major inventions by which biophilic architecture increases resilience. Although some of these
pathways are well-established connections, others are more uncertain and warrant further research and
discoveries.
